blocks.x: The End The End Anyway, I only knew Tommy about six months before he died. Very nice fellow, very quiet.
Very nice. He wasn't doing me for years.
Nobody knew he had a bad heart at that time, but he had a bad heart and just found him dead one day. At least he didn't suffer much.
Yeah, that was good.

I'm working on some material now on Jolly Roll Morton, who was one of my favorite pianists, and of course he wrote a lot of pieces, and I just figured that anyone in the business, as long as you would have known him...
I know him when he first came here from New Orleans. I was working at the Monaco in... Yes, it was.
Was that on 31st Street or...?
35th.
35th?
Uh-huh. I had my teeth wet in, I can't talk to you. Yes, when he first came here, he came here with Billy Mac. They had a little show and he came here from...

Which was the Mary Mac and Billy Mac. Mary Mac and Billy Mac. And I once interviewed them for Tulane University. They live right down the street. Yeah. And... Punch used to remember Punch Miller, trumpet player from the audience, he... his first records he made with the Macs, and he traveled with them in the show. Johnny Dodd said he traveled with them, too.
And I had a letter, I was just looking for it. I had a letter here from England, and they tried to get some daughter on... on him. And, you know, he worked with me, too.

Johnny Dodds? Yes. Oh, yes. I knew him and Baby I knew very well. Yes, well, Baby was a drummer. Yes, I knew him. But Johnny was a clown in his face. Yes. I was just thinking about Johnny when I rode down with my friend. I said, now, Johnny used to have a house, an apartment house. His widow lost that soon after he died, but about in the 40-hundred block.
Down this...
On Michigan, I think, on the other side. Yes.
Well, Johnny played clarinet with me after my clarinet player died.
Oh, Bryant. Yes, Jimmy O' Bryant. I have quite a few of the records that you made with Johnny and with Tommy Ladner.
I have a bunch of them there.
Oh, yeah, those lovely Austin Sirenators.
And then I'm just completely working with another firm. I have the record back there. I'll show you. I've forgotten the name of the firm. I've got it back there.
I was trying to think, did you make, just a few years ago, a Riverside record when they came here? That's it. That's it. Because we were talking about Lil Armstrong. I interviewed her.
Yes, she made it on the same time I did.
Yes, she had the talking record that she had.

Alberta came here with me. Alberta. I sent a letter from Alberta. She's back in New York. I never really knew her. I never really knew her. Well, she was on her way to Denver when she stopped here. I never really knew her. Well, she was a cargoer, and I sent her away from me to New York, because she went on the show.
That's where I first saw her. It was in about 1940 in New York.

That's when she went for the show. And she went to Paris, and she stayed there. Yes. Well, I've never seen her since. But she's back now. She's working at the hospital there in New York. Oh, really? She and I are very good friends, and I hear from her about every week or two. Yes. I hear from her. And every time she comes here, she comes here with me.
If you don't mind, tell me, where were you born? Right here in Chicago?
No, I was born in Chattanooga, Tennessee.
Well, Chattanooga. I should have known it. I've no doubt read notes about you, too, but I just couldn't think, you know, whether I knew you didn't come from, say, way down south of New Orleans.
You probably knew my father, because he was a great musician and a teacher in New York. Did you know Professor Calvin?

No, I wasn't around New York very long, actually, and I didn't get to meet many musicians there. Although I did know, for instance, as I say, Tommy Ladner, and I knew, well, that's one place where I'd met Jolly Row Martin in Washington, and he came to, just the last couple of years of his life is when I knew him, only 1938 when I met him, and he died in 41.

Well, I went to work at the Monogram in 1913. In 13? And I worked at 34th Street until they moved to 35th Street, and I moved there with him. That's the first time I went to New York, and I came right back and stayed down there when I worked there 25 years straight. And then I went to New York and started working for Herdic and Seaman. I was taking high fast shows, and I worked for Herdic and Seaman for a long time. And then I came, when I came home, my mother died in 31. So I just came on the stage. You stayed here then all that time? And I was working at a studio downtown. I knew you'd been, yes.
I knew John Steiner told me you were playing piano for a dance studio.

Yeah, Jimmy Payne. Then I worked for him 17 years. Yes, I knew you'd been there. And then I worked for another woman, a white woman who had a studio down there at Jackson Boulevard, 22, East Jackson. Oh, yes. And then I got sick. I was in the hospital for four or five months, and I came out. My sister just died in November, in April. She'd been there almost two years now. Well, she had been there two years. Yes, you think this is that you have. So I haven't been doing anything since my sister died. I just stayed home. My brother-in-law and I live here together. My sister's southern. But other than that, I've been doing pretty good. You're looking fine, really. I had all my teeth taken out and I just got my teeth back. And, well, I've been doing all right. So this author of the stuff that just put me down in the bed and I couldn't walk.
I went to see Ike Robinson who had played with Jolly Roll for a while, the banjo player. And his wife was having trouble with her teeth. But I had a nice interview. That was two days ago.
You knew Jolly Roll, didn't you?
I knew him. I met him only about four times.

Oh, you didn't meet him when he was young. Not when he was young. I remember when he first came here. What was he like? He had a little bottom pass. Really? He had a big cowboy hat. He was kind of a clown-like, you know.
But a very, very talented musician.
Oh, I thought so too.
I liked his piano playing.
And, well, you know, he didn't know our music.
He didn't really read music much.
No, no. Not much. No, not at all.
But when was that, when you were at the monogram first, when you first met him? I know it's hard to remember the exact year.
I just can't remember, but it was in the 20s.

It would be in the 20s. You did a meeting back in, say, 1915 or so, because he did have one of his blues was published, the Jolly Roll Blues. Rossiter published that in 1915. Yes. That was the first one. And I just wondered if you would have known those.
It might have been around, it might have been around then, because we named Jolly Roll Blues. Mm-hmm. And I used to take down all of his music for him, because he couldn't read music.
Couldn't read music. When he first came here he didn't? Yes.
No, he couldn't read no music. He wouldn't know a note if he'd get on a telegraph for all the legs, like that. And when he was here, he wrote...
Oh, there were a lot of those pieces.
I mean, that one...

Like Wolverine was one of the famous ones. That's it. That's what I was thinking. And the Pearls, I liked that. I heard him play that the first time I went to see him. I asked him to play the Pearls, and he did.
You know, I took down all of his music for him. He kept it all in his head. All in his head. Mm-hmm. Couldn't read it. And he would come... I didn't live here then. I lived at 33, 33, 36, in Calumet.
In Calumet, over... Not so far from the Sunset and the Plantation down in those...
Right down in the street.
Mm-hmm.
I used to work at the Sunset.
You did there too?

Mm-hmm. And Jelly Roll would come, and he would stay two and three hours, and I would take his music all down from him and make all of his copies. That's the way he got copies, it's the half-post. He'd have no way to take it down. And he wouldn't trust nobody but me.

Well, don't blame him, because people could steal it. I know Tony... I never knew Tony Jackson, but I knew Tony's sister I met here, Mrs. Sutter. And she said too that people would steal that music from Tony sometimes if he didn't care whether he had it published or not.
Irvin Barleen did a couple of pieces. Somebody took some of Tony's, I guess.
Irvin Barleen did himself.
Really? Tony worked right next to Tony, a little one with a beer johnson. And Irvin used to come out here and sit for hours with Tony.
Listen to Tony.
Listen to Tony. Pretty Baby and all that stuff. That's all Tony's.
Oh, yes. That was his biggest hit, I guess.
Yes. Pretty Baby. But this boy was very nice, he was a hit. And I would take down his numbers for him.
You see, he wore sort of sport clothes and all that.
Yes, a big bell-bottled pants. And a big hat. Mm-hmm. And he was very loud mouth.
But it was nice. I know you used to brag a lot, but still he was a wonderful musician, I thought. Oh, he was a wonderful musician. If I could have played like he did, I would brag too.
I don't think they'll ever have one that'll play right off the record like he did.
You made a lot of those early records. Some people think they sound like old-time ragtime, but I like that style.
Well, they do. They do. But that was all we knew then.
Yes, that's right. In those days.

Mm-hmm. That's when I started making records. Sort of the ragtime period. That's when I started making records. And he was very interesting. He was a very nice fellow. And he joined Mary Mack. And I was just sitting here trying to think. I don't know whether one time he came in. Mary Mack used to always have little dance bands, and she would bring them up with her show.
Yes. The Mutt Carry. Do you remember Mutt Carry came up with Johnny Dodds in a four-piece band with Mary and Mary Mack?
With Mary Mack.
Mm-hmm. And then Punch came up with them.
Well, they came right to the monogram.
Yes, I know they would have been there tomorrow.
That's where they played.
Which way, which side of the street was the monogram was on 35th, you said?
On this side of the street.
Or was it on State Street? On State Street.
On State. 35th and 6th. About three doors from 35th Street. 35th.
I knew the Graham Theater. No, no, that's at 31st.
That's down there where the old monogram is.
Yeah, and I knew the Vendome, where Erskine Tate used to play. That was at 35th. I don't think they ever saw the monogram.
Well, the monogram down at 31st Street closed when they opened the monogram at 35th.
They had had one at 31st Street, then they moved it on up.
Then they moved it to 35th Street. That was before my time.
I was that old, but I wasn't in Chicago then.
Mm-hmm, well, I was around, when I first came here, I came to 31st, that was in 1913. Mm-hmm. Just going into 1913.
When Jelly Roll came here, they already had the monogram at 35th. At 35th. 35th already. Yes. And he came there. You don't remember when they moved about?
They moved, do you mean when they moved the monogram? Yes, the monogram. They moved the monogram, I think I stayed at 31st Street, about three years.
Maybe around 1916 or so.

They might have moved. Right around in there. Mm-hmm. Because, no, it wasn't. Because when they moved the monogram, 35th Street, yes, it was, because I had bought my house then at 33rd. And I bought that in 19 and 19, that's when I moved that, in 1919. 1919. Yes, that's when I moved to 35th Street. That was one of the first colored families that moved over there, because Pony Moe. I know you've heard of Pony Moe. Yes. Well, Pony Moe lived over there, and I moved over there after he moved, after he died.
Mm-hmm.
And I was one of the first ones that moved over there. And then I moved over to South Park, that's when they started building that theater there.
The Riggle?

Riggle, yeah. And then I moved from South Park over to the, that's the one, 31. Yes. That's right down the street near, right off of 31st Street. I bought that house from Charlie Gomeske, that owned the baseball park. Oh, yes. All the kids were there. The White South. I mean the baseball. The White South. And I lived there until my mother died. Well, my mother died, I just couldn't live there, so I won't see it.
No, it's good to have a change in the case of that. That was in 31. Then you moved out here.
And I haven't seen Jell-E Roll since then. I'd always kind of keep up with him wherever he would be and what he was doing.

And he went on to New York. Yes, I did. And then during the Depression he didn't have very good luck. He was in Washington when I met him and playing in a little night club there and helping run the club, but he didn't like it. And he stayed there until 1938. Then he went away back to New York in 39. And I only saw him once in New York up at the rhythm club where the musicians would all hang out. Yes. He played pool there a lot.
Well, I was in New York for a long, long time. Four years I was out there. But I didn't see him.
You didn't run into him?
No.
Did you ever play any jobs with him or did he ever work in your band or anything?
No, he didn't work in my band. He worked with me and Mac's band.
Yes.
But he worked in the theater where.

In the theater where you were then? That's where I was. You were in the pit orchestra sort of there? Yes. I remember people tell me, and I did once hearing, Manzi Campbell. Yes, the drummer. He worked with you, didn't he, for a long time?
Oh, I knew Manzi. Manzi came from Bill Cassancho. Oh, is that right? That's where he was. He and his brother. He had a brother that played there.
They called him Bunker, I believe.
No.
A violinist, was it?
No, he was a saxophone player. Oh, is that right? I was thinking of him. No, he was a saxophone player. He was a violin player. His mother was named Dutch.
Dutch. They called her Dutch. Oh, who was that? His mother. His mother. Oh, his mother. He used to call her Dutch. But he was supposed to have had a brother, I'd heard.
He had a brother, but his brother was a saxophone player. A saxophone player. Mm-hmm. Because Bill Cassancho and his wife lived in Chattanooga, where I used to live. They were from Chattanooga?
No, they weren't.

They were from New Orleans. But Bill Cassancho's wife's sister married one of my friends, one of them. They were from Chattanooga. So that's where he got the move. And they moved to Chattanooga. Mm-hmm. No, Bill Cassancho, his wife, his wife's sister, that used to be on the show, and she married a seventh
boy in Chattanooga. So when they moved there with his mother.
I didn't know Billy Cassands was from New Orleans. I'd heard people talk about him. A lot of the old time, Laudville people talk about his act.

They're both from New Orleans. They were from New Orleans. Mm-hmm. His wife and I were very good friends. But, now I'm not so positive for sure that he was from New Orleans or not. But I know his wife was.
Yes. At least they were from way down in the deep south.

And I think he was from there. I know his wife was from there. From New Orleans. His wife and I were very, very good friends. She's dead now. She lives in Chattanooga. And whenever she'd come here to Chicago, she'd always live with me.
Mm-hmm.
Because we were good friends. We had no one. And she didn't know nobody in Chicago.
Mm-hmm.
And she's dead now.
Yes. Well, I guess Billy Cassands had been dead for years.
Oh, yes.
I never did get the same. I never did. Very, very funny. Mm-hmm. People used to tell me about it.
Now, a Jolly Roll, what Mary would do, because she had very few musicians that could read music.

Well, are the Macs still here, by the way? Yes. You know, I should talk to them again, too, because I did interview them, but I didn't talk to them about Jolly Roll. I never thought about it at that time. Well... That was ten years ago when I talked to them.

Well, Jolly Roll worked them. They brought them here, but what she would do, because her musicians couldn't read music, most of them. Yes. So she would have them learn the show. Then she'd bring the show now.
Yes.
And of course they had a circuit pin for a color show called Toby. The T-O-B-A, yes.
Yeah, T-O-B-A, yes. Mm-hmm. And she would bring them on that show. Travel all over there on that. And... So Jolly Roll played in her band then. He certainly did.
Piano and...
And Jimmy Dodd played in the band. Johnny Dodds.
I mean Johnny Dodds. Yeah, Johnny Dodds. Not Baby Dodds. I didn't know. No, I don't think Baby came up with King Oliver. Yes.
To join King Oliver here. Yes. And King Oliver, he went over on the gardens, the Royal Gardens.
Yes, the Royal Gardens. And I think he played at the Pekin, the old Pekin and the Dreamland too.
No, I don't think he played at the Dreamland.
Louis Armstrong played at the Dreamland. He did there, I guess.
That's where Lil... That's where he married Lil.
Yes, with Lil. He was married to Lil.
Keppert, I believe she said was there once. Jimmy Keppert. Yeah, or no, wait, Freddie. Freddie Keppert. Freddie Keppert.
Freddie, Freddie across the street. They had a cafe across the street.
Was there Deluxe or something?
Yes, I think they...
There was an entertainer's up in that section.
No, in the entertainers was the 31st Street. Yes, the 31st Street.
Near Indiana, I believe someone told me.
Yes, just off of Indiana. Just down from the...
Can you remember how Jellie played in those days? Did he play any solos when you first heard him or... Yes, he would play in the band.

See, they would play the show. For the max. And then they would play, you know, some kind of little something that they have together, because they got all this stuff together. Yeah. Nobody could take it but them because nobody knew it.
Yeah.

And then if he had a piece that he'd write, he would say, Lovey, I want you to come and help me with this. I'd say, all right. And he'd come over to my house and he'd stay there for hours and hours and hours.
That's when you lived down near 31st Street down in there? 33rd. Third. 33rd.
I would take it down firm on paper. And then when I would finish it, he'd always pay me. He always had money. And how he did, I don't know.
I guess he used to gamble a lot sometimes, really, Sam. Nobody did.
I didn't see him. I never saw him gamble.
He was a great pool player, people tell me.
Well, if he was, I never saw him. If he played pool, I didn't even see him. And I never saw him gamble.
No, you wouldn't have been around those places. No.

And then, too, I... But he always had money. If he wanted his work done, if he wanted his work done, he would come and I would do it. And then he would tell me, I'm going out of town and I got a number I want you to take down for me, and I'll be back. He couldn't take it down himself. So he'd come back and he'd get me to take it down for him. And he thought I was the finest musician in the world, the best friend he had, and I felt that way about him.

I'm sure if he could trust you, he would appreciate it. Yeah, because I didn't want to love the music. I had more than my own, and I could do it. Do you remember any of the pieces in particular? You said maybe... I took down the Wolverine. The Wolverine would be for it.
And I took down two or three other pieces from him, but I can't now think of what they were. I have a few. I know one of them was a song.
The very first piece he wrote and had published was the original Jelly Roll Blues.
Yes, that's when he got that name.

At Rossiter published that. Oh, one time Jelly told some friends of mine that that name Jelly Roll was given to him here in Chicago. Right here, I gave it to him. You really? Yes, because I was making records.
I was just getting ready to start making records. And it was called Jelly Roll. He wasn't named Jelly Roll then, but... What is his first name? Fred?
Ferd. Ferd. Ferdinand.
Yeah, now you see, I remember that first of him. It was a long time, and I can't remember where back then. That wasn't his name. So we named him Jelly Roll.

Yes, certainly. And he also told these people, I was going to say, that he used to sometime be on the stage. Did you ever see him on any kind of an act? I never saw him on the stage. That he would ever try to sing, or maybe like a comedian. I never saw him. I don't think...
He was a very, very good talent, didn't he? I thought so too, yeah. But very, very unfortunate with money. He didn't know how to keep money. Just didn't keep his money, huh? No, no.
It's probably true that people told me he gambled maybe a lot.
I don't know what he did. I never saw him gamble. But I know every time I turned around, he was writing on me. Miller was the one at the theaters.
Oh, he was the manager of the theaters. Uh-huh. He owned them. He owned both of them. He owned both of them.
He used to own half of 31st Street. Really? From 31st Street to 29th. On that side of the street, you owned most all the houses and they had a saloon there. It's 29th and State.
Estate?
No, 30th and State.
30th and State.
Just on the other side of the Monogram.
Miller, what was his first name?
Can you remember? I can't think of this person. His son still owns the building right here on the corner. Oh, really?
They're still around the family? Old man Miller.
Miller. I worked for him 25 years. And when I went down to, in Alabama with the show, the show, that's when he bought the grand.
He had the grand too then? Oh yes, he bought the grand. Yeah.

And when I went down in Alabama, I was trying to get my people all back home because we got caught in the flood down in Spreeport. And old man Miller sent me 20-month tickets. Who else was on the show with you? Did you ever travel with Ida Cox?

I know you made all those records with her. Oh yes, I suppose I was. She was here, you know. She has people over here on the water. She just died, I guess, a year or so ago. Is she dead? She died, yes.
I read about it. And she lived in Nachter. Yeah, she lived down in there.

That must have been where she died. Her daughter had talked to Google down there. And she'd been there, Tennessee. Her daughter had talked to Google down there. I didn't really know her. I heard her a couple of times. I know I put her on the records. I heard her, of course, on all your records. I put her on the records.
I put her on the records. I put her on the records.

I put them on the records. I put them on the records. I have her records, but I never got to meet her or see her or hear her in person. Well, she died. She was great. But she was from Georgia. She was from Columbus.
She was from Columbus, too.
Around Columbus, too. Yeah, and she was with me for years. Which was your favorite blues singer? Who did you like best, their voice and all?
Well, I worked with either London than I did anybody else, so I guess I would probably have to say that. But Maureen was a singer that, when I was a little girl...
I like that deep quality that she had, that big, heavy voice. Maureen?
When I was a little girl, I mean a little girl... What's her name there who worked for Columbia?
Bessie Smith. Bessie Smith. Bessie Smith lived right next door to me.
She was raised in my mother's house. She was raised in my mother's house. We were raised together. Well, you know, Bessie made every record that I put out.
She made it on Columbus.
And way Bessie learned how to sing. Maureen and Paureen, that's her husband.
Yes, I've heard it.

They used to come there with a carnival, and it happened in a vacant lot. And Bessie and I used to sit out in the back of the carnival because we couldn't go in. Yeah. We'd sit out there, and Maureen would sing, Oh, these dogs of mine, that's a little torture. Yeah, I remember that. And we would sit back out there, and she would imitate Maureen singing. She would learn. That's the way she learned how to sing. And she was here with me just before she went away. See, she went down to Memphis, and her brother was driving in the car and had an accident.

Yes, sir. There's a man down in New Orleans now, Dave Oxley, that was in that show, told me all about it. Mm-hmm. Did you ever know Clarence Williams in New York? I guess you would have, but I knew him. I knew Clarence Williams here. Oh, when he was last right, he had the music store here.
Right down there on State Street.
He came from New Orleans, of course.
31st and State Street. I knew him here before he ever went to New York.
Of course, Jelly Roll would have known him, too.
Well, I knew him very well.
In late years, that last couple of years of Jelly's life when he was writing music, Clarence Williams was trying to sell the music there, and it was the agent.
Well, Clarence had to do good for everybody that was from Chicago, because that was kind of a syndicate.
They would own everybody.
And, of course, when they wrote St. Louis Brewers.
Yes, the Handley.
When Handley wrote St. Louis Brewers in Memphis, I was there.
Oh, really? You were around at that time?
He worked at White Dixie Park on one side of the fence, and I worked at the Cove Park.
Was that near Beale Street or down in that part? Right on it. Right down there, yes.

He worked over there at the White Park, and he worked over here at the Cove Park. And my house, I was married to Dudley then. I know you've heard of Dudley. Yes, I've heard. I had theatre and... Yes, I've heard the name. Well, that was my first husband. That was your first husband. Yes, and we were brought that theatre there, opened that theatre, bought that theatre. And that's where we separated. And, uh, Klein, the fellow that used to book the shows, whatever, used to book that whole section, he used to come over and he said, Mrs. Dudley, if you ever make up your own mind from Chicago, I want you to write me in the name. I was just thinking about Tommy Ladner.
When was the first time you met him, or when did you start working with him?
Well, Tommy roomed at my house when he first came to his cove. Oh, he roomed with you.
That's right. You told me that, or I heard that some reddit someplace.
Well, he and his mother lived over East End, and his mother got killed. Oh, I didn't know.
I never knew Tommy very well.
Well, his mother got killed, and some mother tried to say that he and his mother, he and some man was fighting, and he shot the man, and the shot killed his mother.
So they had him in trouble for a long time.

Then he came to room with the man. I was living in 33rd then. And he was playing connet. And you know this, I'm trying to think now, what is his name? He's a connet player. He has a band. I said, all right boy. Then he had a garage. What was his name? He taught that boy to play connet right into my house. And finally the boy got in the band. And I went to New York to see my father. That's the first time I went to New York. And one of the boys there that was from New Orleans said, love me, I'm getting ready to go to England. And I haven't got any connet player with that one. And he said, did you get Tommy to work with me? I said, I don't know, I'll find out.
He was with Fletcher Henderson over there for a while. This was before that. Before that, yeah. When he first went.
Yeah, when he was the second time I went there. So he was with Fletcher. Boy Heather made a band there. I think it's Woody something.
I don't know. It was Woody Herman, but he was a clarinet player. No, no, no.
No, this is him.
Oh yeah, I know. I think I know now. Woodward. I know the band. I know who you mean. Well, that's what he said. I think Sidney Bechet was with him maybe for a while too. Yes, Sidney.
Sidney used to work with us when I was Mac Devon.
Well, you.
He said he played clarinet. Yeah, clarinet.
Where did he work with you? It was Dudley with my husband.

Oh, Dudley's place. He used to play in his band. Did he work with you in any theater? No, Dudley was a clarinet player. Yes. And he had a band. Well, Sidney went to New York. I knew him quite well. I remember when the first time he saw snow on the ground, he left to go crazy. He'd never seen snow before. I liked Sidney.
He was a funny fellow too.
And Fletcher, you know him.
He was a real, real, real Creole.
But you knew the best of all of them. Sidney Bessie. Yeah, he was a wonderful fellow.
Oh, boy. Muggsy Spanier. Yeah, well, he, that's his best of all of them. He was the fellow that Tommy would.
Taught. Oh, Muggsy, sure.
Muggsy. Yeah, we couldn't think of him. I couldn't think it all. He learned how to play on him. He's dead now too, you know. Yeah, but he learned how to play on him in my house.
He learned how to play on him in my house.

He's dead now too, you know. Yeah, but he learned how to play on him in my house. Right there, you're from Tommy. Yeah, I can believe that because I know, he told me too, Muggsy, you told me too, Tommy was one of his favorites. He taught him. And when Tommy died, he wrote a little article in Downbeat about him. So he gave him credit as being one of the great ones.
He taught him. I know he used to come there every Saturday and take his lessons.
Do you mind telling how old you are now unless some people don't want to tell me? I'm 83. 83. What was your birth date when you...
19th of September. 19th? 19th of September I will be 83. I'm 82 now.
